title: Hackers Got Inside a Flock Camera. Its Data Shows How the System Really Works
gist: Hackers physically removed a Flock Safety license-plate camera, extracted its on-device encryption key, and handed the data to journalists, revealing that the cameras explicitly detect people (not just plates), generate over a million images in weeks, and feed a national multi-agency search network already tied to ICE and abortion-related police lookups — a security and reputational overhang on Flock's core surveillance-network business model.

themes.theme: The breach: how the encryption was defeated

insights.claim: A hacker collective calling itself stegan0gram physically removed a Flock Safety camera from above a roadway, made a near-complete copy of its stored data, recovered an on-device encryption key, and shared the material with journalists at 404 Media, WIRED, and the transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: A vendor's marketed on-device encryption was defeated by physical device theft plus key extraction — a concrete security failure for a company whose entire value proposition rests on trustworthy custody of sensitive surveillance data.
insights.quote: Hackers ripped down a Flock camera above a roadway, made a near-complete copy of the data stored inside it
insights.locator: Hackers ripped down a Flock camera

insights.claim: The hackers found the Flock camera's Android system had at least two unencrypted storage partitions, 'vendor' and 'media,' and that the 'media' partition contained the encryption key that unlocked the rest of the camera's stored video and image data.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: A specific, reproducible technical flaw (key stored unencrypted alongside the data it protects) is now public, meaning the vulnerability is not theoretical and could be replicated against other deployed units unless patched.
insights.locator: The hackers said they were able to access

insights.claim: A security researcher, Jon 'GainSec' Gaines, had already reverse engineered a Flock license-plate reader in early 2025 and documented flaws enabling root-level access, but Flock acknowledged the findings while downplaying their severity, saying they required physical access and that footage didn't persist on-device long enough to be exposed.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Flock had prior, specific warning of the exact class of vulnerability now shown to be exploitable at scale (physical access leading to data exposure) roughly 18 months before this breach, undercutting the company's earlier public reassurances about severity.
insights.quote: would still not be able to gain access to footage

insights.claim: Analysis of the recovered camera software shows it explicitly detects people, not just vehicles, license plates, and bicycles, recording where a person appears in an image and the system's confidence in that detection — a capability the article says is typically overlooked in public discussion of Flock cameras.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Marketed as a license-plate reader, the device is confirmed to be a general person-detection surveillance sensor as well — materially changes the privacy/regulatory risk profile versus Flock's public framing as a narrow vehicle-tracking tool.
insights.locator: The software running on the camera

insights.claim: Recovered device logs covering about 21 days of camera activity show it photographed roughly 50,200 vehicles and generated about 1.6 million images, averaging around 3,300 vehicles per day with a peak of 4,454 in a single day.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Quantifies the raw data-generation intensity of a single camera unit; at national-network scale (thousands of cameras) this implies enormous aggregate surveillance data volume flowing into Flock's cloud infrastructure and searchable index.
insights.locator: According to our analysis, the camera’s logs

insights.claim: A typical passing vehicle triggers about 28 images from the camera, with some vehicles generating more than 100 images, as the camera captures multiple exposures to isolate both the license plate and the wider scene before cropping and transmitting selected frames.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Confirms plate-reading and object-recognition happen server-side, not on-device — meaning raw imagery (beyond just plate text) is routinely transmitted and stored off-device, expanding the surface area for the kind of data exposure this breach demonstrated.
insights.locator: According to the code, when something moves

insights.claim: When WIRED extracted the camera's detection models and ran them against 27,321 recovered short video clips, the models found people in only 11 clips, all of them motorcyclists, likely because the camera's downward angle over a roadway made pedestrian detection unlikely.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Shows person-detection is functionally present but rarely triggered in this specific roadway-facing camera placement — the risk would scale up meaningfully for cameras positioned to capture pedestrians (e.g., sidewalks, storefronts), which is a placement-dependent risk variable worth tracking as deployments expand.

insights.claim: The camera's license-plate detector produced false positives in testing, mistaking bumper stickers, dealership frames, and other graphics for plates, including cropping an American flag patch on a motorcyclist's saddlebag as if it were a license plate.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Demonstrates real-world false-positive rates in the core plate-detection model, a data quality issue relevant to any downstream law-enforcement reliance on the system's outputs for identification or investigation.
insights.locator: The tests also showed how broadly

insights.claim: WIRED and 404 Media found no evidence of active facial-recognition capability in the camera's software beyond default features included in the Android operating system, and those default capabilities did not appear to be enabled or in use.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Partially corroborates Flock's public claim that it does not perform facial recognition, which is a relevant fact for the company's regulatory and reputational defense even as other privacy concerns (person detection, national search network) are confirmed.

themes.theme: The national search network and its controversies

insights.claim: In Alpharetta, Georgia, WIRED found that records from the city's Flock cameras were accessible to more than 2,000 agencies nationwide, including police departments, colleges, airports, and the federal General Services Administration's Office of Inspector General.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: A single local government's camera data reaching 2,000+ outside agencies illustrates how far Flock's cross-agency data-sharing network extends beyond the purchasing jurisdiction's original consent/oversight scope — a core legal and political exposure for the company.
insights.quote: records from the city’s Flock cameras were accessible to more than 2,000 agencies

insights.claim: Flock's national cross-agency search network has previously been reported to have been used by local police performing lookups on behalf of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, including in areas that had banned cooperating with immigration authorities or exporting license-plate data out of state, and by a Texas officer who searched the network nationwide for a woman who had self-administered an abortion.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Establishes documented cases of Flock's network being used to circumvent local sanctuary/data-export policies and for reproductive-health-related surveillance — concrete legal and political liability precedent that could drive municipal contract cancellations or new state legislation restricting the network.

insights.claim: In August 2026, WIRED obtained frontend code for Flock's police-facing software, now called OS Investigate (previously Nightshift), and reconstructed portions of the tool, showing it can identify drivers, surface vehicles that repeatedly travel together, and search for people based on movement patterns by combining camera records with police files and commercial data.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Confirms the analytical layer on Flock's servers goes well beyond simple plate lookups into pattern-of-life and associate-network analysis by fusing camera data with police and commercial datasets — the kind of capability that draws the most regulatory scrutiny for law-enforcement AI tools.
insights.locator: In August, WIRED obtained frontend code

insights.claim: Multiple people have been arrested across the US for allegedly tampering with or sabotaging Flock cameras, some towns have announced they will stop using Flock cameras altogether, and one police department built a fake 3D-printed Flock camera case specifically to bait potential vandals.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Physical sabotage and municipal contract cancellations are an active, ongoing customer-and-legal risk to Flock's installed base and growth pipeline, not just a hypothetical PR concern.
insights.locator: Across the country, multiple people have been arrested

insights.claim: One of the hackers said their motivation was to reverse engineer and expose the cameras' inner workings rather than simply destroy them, framing the act as liberating hardware and disarming a surveillance system, while acknowledging concern about being investigated and trying to stay low-profile.
insights.speaker: stegan0gram hacker (quoted by Dhruv Mehrotra)
insights.so_what: Signals the emergence of a more sophisticated adversary class (technical reverse-engineering and public disclosure, not just vandalism) targeting surveillance-camera vendors, which raises the bar and frequency of future security disclosures Flock and peers will face.
insights.quote: Why just destroy them when we can reverse engineer them and find the secrets of those spying on us?
insights.locator: one of the hackers, from a collective

insights.claim: A former police officer and outspoken Flock critic warns that vigilante sabotage of cameras could backfire by strengthening the state's argument that the surveillance tool is necessary, and argues that continued escalation is a direct consequence of officials ignoring public objections to the technology.
insights.speaker: Noel Pichardo
insights.so_what: An insider critique that the anti-surveillance backlash strategy (sabotage) may be counterproductive politically, suggesting the more durable path to curbing Flock's network is legislative/policy pressure rather than device destruction — relevant to how the regulatory risk plays out over time.
insights.quote: I think that type of vigilantism will only crystallize the police and the state at large in their belief that this tool is necessary.

insights.claim: In response to the breach, a Flock spokesperson said the unauthorized removal and tampering of a camera is illegal, and that the company received no vulnerability report through its official disclosure process and could not assess the claims based on the limited information provided.
insights.speaker: Flock Safety spokesperson (quoted by Dhruv Mehrotra)
insights.so_what: Flock's official response focuses on the legality of the hackers' actions rather than substantively addressing the specific encryption-key flaw, a defensive posture that may not satisfy customers or regulators evaluating the severity of the exposure.
insights.quote: The unauthorized removal and tampering of a Flock camera is illegal.
insights.locator: A Flock spokesperson said in a statement

insights.claim: The camera's recovered logs show significant operational instability, including more than 27,000 'no space left on device' errors while trying to save full-resolution images, plus tens of thousands of related errors, crashes, and reboots.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Points to hardware/storage reliability issues in the deployed camera fleet beyond the security flaw itself, a secondary operational-risk signal for a company whose product durability and uptime underpin its recurring-revenue surveillance-as-a-service model.
insights.quote: more than 27,000 “no space left on device” errors
